title: Sugar
subtitle: 1900–1970 · Glut, War and Quota: The Sugar Trust, Colonial Taiwan, Rationing, Cuba and the First Doubts

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The world wars and sugar, Cuba’s unrest and revolution

entries.label: The war of 1914 cuts Britain off from German beet
entries.hint: Before 1914 Britain drew four-fifths of its sugar from European beet, mostly German and Austrian; the war ends that overnight, the government scours Java, Mauritius, Cuba and the Caribbean for cane, and rationing becomes ‘a working-class complaint’ for the rest of the war. Jam, rum and sugared tea feed the trenches: Robert Graves’s first meal at the front is bread, bacon, rum and tea ‘sickly with sugar’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin, Sugar: The World Corrupted (2017) ch.12 (the 80 per cent from beet, the quotation from Graves). See o2, o3.

entries.label: The crash of 1929 brings unrest and revolution to Cuba’s sugar
entries.hint: After the Wall Street Crash the impact on Cuba’s sugar industry is ‘catastrophic’, with unrest, revolution and the physical takeover of American-owned plantations and mills; Washington’s answer, worried about the danger of upheaval, is the quota system of 1937 (o7).
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11 (he gives no years for the unrest beyond ‘after the Wall Street Crash of 1929’; the bracket 1930–33 is mine). The fall of the Machado government in 1933 is general knowledge and not in the source.

entries.label: The U-boats make sugar scarcer than meat in British minds
entries.hint: European beet is again under German control and imported cane faces the submarines of the Battle of the Atlantic; sugar is rationed in Britain at 12 oz a person a week from January 1940 and the rations are cut as the war bites. A shop assistant in Dewsbury notes that sugar ‘seems even more than tea to be the thing people would like more of’, and that men are ‘the sugar devourers’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (Kathleen Hey’s wartime diary). See o7 and l3.

entries.label: Castro seizes the sugar estates and the US cuts Cuba’s quota
entries.hint: After the revolution Castro confiscates the sugar estates of over 1,000 acres and bars foreigners from owning Cuban land; Congress slashes Cuba’s sugar quota, Cuba turns to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as trading partners, and when President Kennedy bans all trade the US at once loses half of its sugar supplies.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11 (he dates the revolution ‘1958’; the years 1959–62 are a bracket of mine for the confiscations, the quota cut and the embargo). See o9 and x1.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Brussels Convention, colonial Taiwan, wartime commissions and rationing, Tate not State and the US Sugar Act

entries.label: The Brussels Convention tries to end beet-sugar bounties
entries.hint: The Brussels Sugar Convention of 1902 aims to end state support for exported sugar — the bounties that had kept European beet cheap and driven the price down — by limiting surtaxes and requiring members to admit sugar from participating states at their lowest rates if those states paid no bounties. It is often called the first multilateral commodity agreement.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (web summaries only; none read in full): a FRUS extract and Moura Filho’s 2006 MPRA paper on the origin of international commodity agreements. The treaty text and the bounty system’s details were not read; the claim ‘first multilateral commodity agreement’ is the abstract’s. Compare Mazumdar, Sugar and Society in China (1998) pp.382–383 on the glut of 1900–14.

entries.label: Japan’s colonial rules turn Taiwan into ‘another Java’
entries.hint: The ‘Regulations for the Encouragement of the Sugar Business’ of 1902 subsidise land bought for cane and 20 per cent of the cost of machinery, give each factory a licensed district, and require all cane in a district to go to the one factory; by 1905 the state bans the grinding of cane on the old two-roller buffalo mills. Takekoshi wrote that they were meant to turn Formosa into another Java.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.377–379 (her notes 192–199). See te3.

entries.label: Britain founds a Royal Commission for Sugar Supplies
entries.hint: Within days of the declaration of war in 1914 the British Government establishes a Royal Commission for Sugar Supplies; it begins state involvement in the buying, distribution and pricing of sugar that, Walvin says, lasted through much of the century — and, after the war, subsidies to beet growers that supported the British sugar industry for sixty years.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12. See c1, o5.

entries.label: America rations sugar for the war, and Americans save 775,000 tons
entries.hint: When the US enters the war in 1917 its Food Administration tells hotels, clubs and confectioners to cut sugar from the 90 lb a head Americans were using, the US Government and refiners create a monopoly in sugar buying, and in 1918, after German submarines have sunk millions of pounds, a sugar corporation is empowered to import and control it and each person is limited to an ounce a day. Americans were asked to save 600,000 tons and saved 775,000.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11; the Sugar Trust was unpopular for its wartime profits.

entries.label: Britain starts to subsidise home-grown beet and forms Tate & Lyle
entries.hint: From 1921 the British government promotes a British beet-sugar industry to avoid the wartime dependence on European beet, and increases cane imports from imperial sources — Australia, South Africa and Fiji; taxpayers’ money goes to beet farmers, and the same year Tate and Lyle is formed from two competing firms, becoming the dominant force in refining.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (the 1921 start of the promotion and the formation of Tate and Lyle ‘in 1921’).

entries.label: Iran taxes tea and sugar to build its railway
entries.hint: Reza Shah’s Trans-Iranian Railway, joining the Caspian to the Gulf over 1,394 kilometres between 1927 and 1938, is built on state funds raised from taxes on tea and sugar — a case where the consumption of sugar, not its production, paid for a modernising state.
entries.note: SECONDARY (via this atlas): modern-near-east-1900-1945::te1 (‘built on state funds from taxes on tea and sugar between 1927 and 1938’); that entry’s own source was not re-checked here. See ec14.

entries.label: The Chadbourne Agreement tries to restrict world sugar output
entries.hint: After the breakdown of the 1902 convention and a glut of sugar, a 1931 agreement named for Thomas Chadbourne sets export quotas for the main producers to restrict output; it began with American and Cuban interests facing discrimination and was meant to lapse in 1935, and the League of Nations’ International Sugar Agreement of 6 May 1937 followed.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (web summaries only): a Taylor & Francis chapter and the description of Sugar and the Making of International Trade Law (Cambridge) as found by search; the year 1931 and the International Sugar Agreement date of 6 May 1937 are from those pages’ metadata. The terms were not read.
keywords: League of Nations International Sugar Agreement

entries.label: The United States Sugar Act of 1937 regiments the sugar market
entries.hint: Worried about upheaval in Cuba, Franklin Roosevelt compromises with an equal quota in the US market for US-grown and foreign sugar, Cuba getting 64 per cent of the foreign quota; the Sugar Act of 1937 stays in force until 1974 and ‘made sugar the most regimented of all American crops’. US growers, strong in Washington, had also won tariffs on cheap imported sugar.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11. Earlier quota laws of 1934 are not in the source.

entries.label: Britain rations sugar for thirteen years
entries.hint: Sugar rationing begins in January 1940 and lasts, with one brief interlude, until 1953; an Act of 1942 puts the national scheme in the hands of a division of the Ministry of Food. Sweets were de-rationed in 1949, but demand was so immediate that rationing had to be re-introduced for another four years.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (for the system). See c3.

entries.label: ‘Tate not State’: Labour’s plan to nationalise sugar is beaten off
entries.hint: The post-war Labour Government puts sugar on its list of essential industries for nationalisation alongside railways, coal, steel and health, but Tate and Lyle launches a campaign of publicity and propaganda — ‘Tate Not State’, with the cartoon figure of ‘Mr Cube’ — restructures the company to shield its shareholders and the plan is rebuffed. Walvin notes the irony that the firm had long depended on state protection and subsidy.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (the years are the span of the Attlee government, not Walvin’s). See e1.

entries.label: Congress slashes Cuba’s sugar quota
entries.hint: After Castro’s land seizures the US Congress ‘promptly’ cuts Cuba’s quota and, with Kennedy’s trade ban, gives it to American producers, lifting the 26-year-old restrictions on US cane growing: the growers were ‘given the green light to plant as much sugar as they could grow’, which led to Florida’s sugar boom.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11 (‘26-year-old restrictions’ implies 1934, and the year of the cut is not given, so 1960 is a general-knowledge placement). See c4, ec14.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Graves at the front, Mr Cube, sweetened cereals for children and convenience food

entries.label: Graves’s first meal at the front is bread, bacon, rum and sugared tea
entries.hint: Robert Graves, leaving his public school to join the army in 1914, remembers his first meal at the front as ‘bread, bacon, rum and bitter-stewed tea sickly with sugar’; Walvin notes that rum was the gulp of alcohol that gave men a boost before going over the top, and sugar was in the tea, the bread and the rum.
entries.note: ANCHOR (as quoted): Walvin (2017) ch.12 (quoting Graves’s Goodbye to All That).

entries.label: Post sells sweetened cereal to children
entries.hint: The story of sweet products aimed at children begins in 1949 when Post Foods, struggling to sell its breakfast cereals against competition, turns to the children themselves. The Kellogg cereal that began as a ‘health food’ in 1899 had already established the breakfast table as a place for sugar, and Britain had sixty brands of breakfast cereal by 1912.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 and ch.12 (Kellogg 1899; sixty brands by 1912). The details of Post’s product are in later pages of ch.14 not read here.

entries.label: Mr Cube becomes the face of sugar
entries.hint: The cartoon figure Mr Cube, clever icon of Tate and Lyle’s campaign against nationalisation, is seen on buses, placards, newspaper advertisements and bags of sugar and remains a potent commercial image long after the campaign succeeded. The state that had been sugar’s saviour is the one he is deployed against.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (no year given; 1949 is from general knowledge, placed with o9).

entries.label: ‘JUST HEAT AND SERVE’: Time celebrates convenience food
entries.hint: Time magazine’s 1959 article on convenience food carries the headline ‘JUST HEAT AND SERVE’; Walvin points out that those eating the new foods were absorbing unacknowledged volumes of sugar, as few convenience foods were made without plenty of it.
entries.note: ANCHOR (as quoted): Walvin (2017) ch.14.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Nutrition science, Keys, Yudkin and the sugar industry’s Harvard review

entries.label: Nutrition science finds sugar ‘devoid of minerals and vitamins’
entries.hint: The early twentieth-century science of nutrition, with its discovery of vitamins, amino acids and mineral elements, alongside the poverty surveys of Charles Booth and Seebohm Rowntree, shows that the diet of the poor is inadequate and that sugar is wholly devoid of minerals and vitamins; school dentists find the damage to children’s teeth. Doctors, though, still said sugar was important for ‘muscle-force’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (the bracket 1900–14 is mine, the source says ‘early twentieth century’). See l1.

entries.label: Keys’s six countries make fat the villain
entries.hint: In 1953 the American physiologist Ancel Keys draws attention to a suggestive relationship between fat intake in six countries and their death rate from coronary disease, the first proponent of the idea that fat could cause coronary thrombosis; by 1956 he accepts that animal and vegetable fats differ. Yudkin says that the international statistics could as well have pointed to sugar.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Yudkin, Pure, White and Deadly (1986) pp.84–85 (Yudkin’s own account of Keys, written as an interested party).

entries.label: Yudkin points to sugar in the international heart-disease statistics
entries.hint: In 1957 John Yudkin, professor of physiology and later of nutrition at Queen Elizabeth College, reports that international statistics suggest sugar consumption is at least as interesting as fat to look at in connection with coronary disease — not a proof, but ‘a clue’; a Japanese researcher soon confirms the relationship in 20 countries. His earlier book on weight reduction (1958) had made little distinction between starch and sugar.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Yudkin (1986) p.86 and the front matter (his posts: Professor of Physiology 1945–54 and of Nutrition and Dietetics 1954–71). The 1957 paper’s title and journal are not given in the page read. Yudkin’s account is partisan.

entries.label: The sugar industry pays Harvard scientists to blame fat
entries.hint: In 1967 the New England Journal of Medicine publishes a review by Harvard nutrition scientists that blames fat, not sugar, for heart disease and recommends cutting fat from American diets, without disclosing that the sugar industry’s research foundation had sponsored it; the sponsorship came to light in internal documents published in September 2016. The authors of that exposure say there is no evidence the foundation edited the manuscript, only circumstantial evidence that its interests shaped the conclusions.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 (‘launched in 1967’; ‘exposed in September 2016’); web coverage of Kearns, Schmidt and Glantz, JAMA Internal Medicine (2016). The review’s authors and the amount paid (reported in later coverage as about $50,000 in today’s dollars) were not confirmed from the paper, which was not read; the Sugar Association replied that the foundation should have been more transparent but that disclosure norms differed then.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The glut of 1900–14, Hong Kong and Taiwan, Cuba and the Spanish Caribbean, Coca-Cola, British consumption, supermarkets and Florida

entries.label: Coca-Cola is the world’s biggest industrial buyer of sugar
entries.hint: American soft-drink consumption rises from 0.6 gallons a head in 1889 to 3.3 in 1929; by 1900 every 6 fl oz serving of the Atlanta drink holds four teaspoons of sugar, and Coca-Cola, whose price stayed at five cents from 1886 to 1950, is by 1910 ‘the largest industrial consumer of sugar in the world’. By 1930 more than 7,000 bottling plants fill 6 billion bottles.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (the ‘largest consumer’ quotation is from a source Walvin gives in his notes).

entries.label: Hong Kong’s refineries undercut the Pearl River Delta
entries.hint: Hong Kong refineries processing Javanese and Philippine raw sugar undersell Chinese sugar: prices in China fall by almost half in the decade 1891–1902, Shantou’s exports of nearly 110,000 tons in 1899 have almost stopped by 1911, and the number of sugar-processing units in Guangdong falls from 406 in 1912 to 229 in 1913. Producers switch to rice, vegetables and oil crops.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.383–385 (Maritime Customs reports, her notes 209–218).

entries.label: Five Japanese firms own 70 per cent of Taiwan’s cane land
entries.hint: Under Japanese rule after 1895, a land survey, expropriation of owners who could not prove title, and company tenants and contract smallholders build a capitalist sugar industry: by the 1920s five Japanese corporations own a fifth of all cultivated land and 70 per cent of the land under cane, and the ‘Big Six’ dominate; of 147 Chinese companies in the first decade of the century only 7 survive after 1911. A 1920s folk song says ‘Sweet is Taiwan sugar, but bitter is the life of a cane farmer’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.338 (the folk song), 377–381 (the figures, her notes 187–204). Compare o2.

entries.label: The sugar glut of 1900–1914 breaks smallholder cane
entries.hint: A crisis of overproduction and falling prices hits as dozens of new producers come to market: the Philippines exports about 350,000 tons by 1914, Java almost 1,250,000, and German, Austrian and Californian beet, Cuban cane after 1898, and Hawaii, Fiji, Australia and Natal add to the glut; London raw sugar falls from 25s 6d a hundredweight in 1872 to 7s 3d in 1902.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.382–383 (her notes 206–208).

entries.label: Britain’s biscuit and chocolate factories use sugar by the ton
entries.hint: By 1900 Huntley and Palmer make 400 varieties of biscuit and Peek Freans 200; around 1914 Fry, Cadbury and Rowntree each turn over more than £1 million, with factories, railway sidings and model villages; the average Briton eats 11 oz of sugar a week, and British consumption rises from 68 lb to 90 lb between 1880 and 1914.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12.

entries.label: Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic make 6.75 million tons
entries.hint: After the war of 1898 Cuban output ‘skyrockets’ with new milling methods and American money — by 1919 Americans control about 40 per cent of the industry — and Cuba’s 3.5 million tons of 1925 is the high point; Walvin has Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic making 1.3 million tons in 1902, double that by 1920 and 6.75 million tons by 1923. Sugar dominates Cuban farming.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.42 (40 per cent American-owned by 1919; 3.5 million tons by 1925); Walvin (2017) ch.11. The two series do not obviously agree for the 1920s: Walvin’s 6.75 million tons is for three islands in 1923.

entries.label: Hawaii’s C&H and the American Sugar Refining Company
entries.hint: Formed in 1906, the California and Hawaii company (C&H) dominates Hawaiian sugar until the 1930s; by 1907 the American Sugar Refining Company controls 97 per cent of refined sugar in America. Smith traces Domino Sugar’s present ownership to both.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) pp.34, 54. See sugar-1800-1900::ec15 for the Sugar Trust’s start.

entries.label: British homes eat 1.1 million tons of sugar by 1938
entries.hint: By 1938 British homes eat 1.1 million tons of sugar directly and another 300,000 tons go into confectionery; about 40 per cent of all sugar is eaten in industrially processed foods, and British consumption has grown fivefold in the century to 1936 and 50 per cent from 1880 to 1939, spread evenly across social classes. Supported by the state and by beet subsidies, a few refiners become ‘a real power in the land’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12. The 91 lb a head is for 1914, from the same chapter; see sugar-1800-1900::ec13.

entries.label: Egypt regains its tariff and protects its sugar industry
entries.hint: In 1930 Egypt regains control of its tariff, lost since the free-trade treaty of 1838, and imposes protective duties; behind them industry grows — textiles above all, but also sugar, cement, chemicals and food processing — in a classic pattern of import substitution. The sugar factories of Upper Egypt, built with vacuum pans from about 1860, were its base.
entries.note: SECONDARY (via this atlas): egypt-1900-1952::e3 and egypt-1798-1900::g5; those entries’ own sources were not re-checked here.

entries.label: American sugar use shifts from kitchen to factory
entries.hint: In the United States the share of sugar used at home falls from 70 per cent in 1934 to 57 per cent in 1944, 44 per cent in 1954 and 38 per cent in 1964, while industrial use climbs to 62 per cent; in West Germany industrial use goes from 55 to 70 per cent between 1957–58 and 1981–82. Yudkin notes that the world’s sugar output rose from 35 million tonnes in 1950 to 70 million in 1970.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Yudkin (1986) pp.36 and 46 (tables; the West German split for 1957–58 is printed in the page read as 55/55, an evident misprint — the industrial 55 is used here and the domestic share read as 45).

entries.label: Florida’s sugar rises from 29,000 tons in 1934 to a million in the mid-1960s
entries.hint: Florida’s sugar was a ‘fledgling’ 29,000 tons in 1934, 175,000 by the 1950s; after Cuba’s quota was cut, agribusiness and Cuban exiles with money and know-how move in at Clewiston, output reaches almost a million tons by the mid-1960s, and the acreage rises from 36,000 in 1955 to 276,000 by 1973. The US Sugar Corporation was launched in the 1930s and expanded in wartime.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11; Smith (2015) p.55 (the US Sugar Corporation at Clewiston in the 1930s).

entries.label: Turkey’s first five-year plan builds state sugar factories
entries.hint: After the world depression the Turkish state takes the lead in industry: the first Five-Year Industrial Plan of 1934–38, drawn up with Soviet advice and credit, builds textile, sugar, paper and iron plants. Sümerbank, founded in 1933, is the vehicle.
entries.note: SECONDARY (via this atlas): turkey-1923-1980::ec2; that entry’s own source was not re-checked here. Sugar was one of several state industries, not the plan’s main aim.

entries.label: Coca-Cola’s wartime sales: ten billion bottles for the US military
entries.hint: In January 1942 General Eisenhower orders monthly supplies of Coca-Cola for the US military, which buys 10 billion bottles between 1941 and 1945; Coca-Cola’s profits reach $25 million in 1944 alone, a blow to Pepsi-Cola, which was not allowed access. After the war it is carried abroad with McDonald’s, US aid programmes and over forty new plants in 1960.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15.

entries.label: Supermarkets and fast food multiply
entries.hint: Britain’s 175 supermarkets of 1958 become 2,110 by 1972, and McDonald’s franchised restaurants grow from 250 in 1960 to 3,000 in 1970; American restaurant portions are four times larger by the 1990s than in 1950. Packaged and ready-made foods, most with ‘copious amounts of added sweeteners’, come to shape what people eat.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 and ch.15. The causal link to sugar is Walvin’s argument.

entries.label: British consumption peaks at 115 lb a head in 1958
entries.hint: After the war British sugar consumption continued to rise, peaking at 115 lb (52.4 kg) a head in 1958, and was still over 40 kg in 1990; the nation had emerged from the war ‘even more wedded to sugary foods than before 1939’. In the USA, calorific sweeteners per head in 1950 were just over 100 lb.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 and ch.15. Yudkin (1986) p.36 gives a world average of about 45 lb in the early 1980s against 11 lb in 1900 and 34 lb in 1957.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Taiwan’s modernised cane, saccharin, tenfold yields and the discovery of high-fructose corn syrup

entries.label: Taiwan’s Rose Bamboo cane and steam mills
entries.hint: The Taiwan Seito Kaisha mill begins grinding in 1901 and the colonial state’s research stations introduce the Hawaiian ‘Rose Bamboo’ cane in 1902, yielding 14 tons of cane to the acre and 3,360 lb of crystallised sugar against 8 tons and 1,064 lb of brown sugar from the native variety; by 1907 over 60 per cent of the cane area is planted with it. By 1908 there are 50 steam-driven factories, and the number of buffalo mills falls from 1,127 in 1901 to 191 in 1911.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.378–381 (her notes 186–203; her ‘1,064 pounds of brown sugar’ and ‘3,360 pounds’ are for an acre).

entries.label: Saccharin goes on sale in the sugar famine of the First World War
entries.hint: Saccharin, discovered in 1879, is sold commercially after 1914 and thrives in the years of wartime sugar shortages; cyclamate follows after 1945, and soft-drink makers use them in early attempts at reduced-calorie versions from the 1950s. The US Senate’s Delaney Clause of 1958 bars any additive found to cause cancer in man or animals.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15; Yudkin (1986) p.33 (the Delaney Clause, 1958). See the next folio for the cyclamate ban and aspartame.

entries.label: Taiwan’s Chia-i–Tainan irrigation system serves 370,500 acres
entries.hint: The Japanese colonial state builds the Kanan (Chia-i–Tainan) irrigation network between 1920 and 1930 for 370,500 acres of prime cane land, drawing some 300,000 farm families into compulsory agricultural associations that fix a three-year rotation of cane, rice, legumes and vegetables by controlling each field’s water.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) p.382 (her note 205). A smaller irrigation project of the first decade and another of 1911 are mentioned on p.379.

entries.label: The sugar from an acre rises tenfold between 1850 and 1950
entries.hint: Geoffrey Masefield estimated that, through new industrial techniques and better cane and beet varieties, the yield of sugar per acre increased tenfold between 1850 and 1950 — an increase unmatched by any other crop; Mazumdar notes it as a cause of the glut and the slump in prices.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) p.383 (her note 207, Masefield’s estimate; not checked against Masefield).

entries.label: High-fructose corn syrup is first made
entries.hint: In 1957 a process is found for making high-fructose corn syrup; at first it is dearer than sugar and only becomes cheap thanks to the 1973 Farm Bill, which guarantees corn farmers a profit, and then the world’s sweetener market is transformed (the next folio).
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (corn sweeteners had been available since the late nineteenth century but ‘the taste was never quite right’).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Hong Kong’s and Taiwan’s trade, Florida’s guest workers, Cuba’s turn to the USSR and Coca-Cola abroad

entries.label: Taiwan sells to Japan under a preferential tariff
entries.hint: As a Japanese colony after 1895 Taiwan can export sugar to Japan under a preferential tariff while also competing in East Asian markets, including mainland China; Japan, with raw sugar from Okinawa and Java, itself exports an average of 64,000 tons by 1915.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.370 and 383 (her note 206).

entries.label: Hong Kong’s refiners draw raw sugar from Java and the Philippines
entries.hint: In the decade 1900–10 Hong Kong’s refineries begin getting all their raw sugar from Java and the Philippines, at much lower prices than from mainland China; the China Navigation Company, a Butterfield and Swire subsidiary, carries all sugar refined at Taikoo to north China, Japan, India and Australia.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.383–384 (her note 212). See ec2.

entries.label: Mexican and West Indian guest workers cut Florida’s cane
entries.hint: The US Government’s wartime agreements with the Mexican and British governments bring Mexicans, Bahamians and Jamaicans to work in US agriculture; by the mid-1960s upwards of 20,000 guest workers, mainly West Indians, cut Florida’s cane for five or six months a year in barracks with poor sanitation and almost no healthcare, which to many looked ‘uncomfortably like a new slave trade’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11 (the dates are brackets from ‘the Second World War’ and ‘the mid-1960s’).

entries.label: Cuba turns to the Soviet Union for its sugar market
entries.hint: When Washington slashes Cuba’s sugar quota in 1960, Cuba turns to new trading partners in Russia and Eastern Europe; President Kennedy’s ban on all trade with Cuba then costs the United States half of its sugar supplies.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11. The 1960 trade agreements and the 1962 embargo are named by year from general knowledge.

entries.label: Coca-Cola spreads abroad with aid-funded sugar and bottling plants
entries.hint: In the 1960s Coca-Cola, under new management, expands massively outside the USA, opening more than forty new plants in 1960 alone and, in the decades after the war, benefitting from US aid programmes that funded overseas projects, including help in growing sugar and citrus fruits and in building bottling plants; per capita US soft-drink consumption reaches 23.4 gallons in 1969.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Hawaii’s territorial status, the Marshall Plan and the Everglades

entries.label: Hawaii becomes a US territory and the planters get their way
entries.hint: Hawaii becomes US territory in 1900, so that its sugar planters can trade freely with the mainland; Walvin says that, in 1900, no other foodstuff was as important in the USA and its international dealings. Hawaiian sugar had grown from 1 per cent of the US market in 1875 to 10 per cent by 1900.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11. See sugar-1800-1900::c4.

entries.label: The Marshall Plan sends Europe American food and pushes it to farm
entries.hint: Between 1947 and 1952 the Marshall Plan pours $13 billion into Europe, much of it in American food, feed and fertiliser; Western European governments resolve to raise their own food production, and by the end of the century Europe is a net exporter of sugar from its subsidised beet.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14; Smith (2015) p.50 (Europe a net exporter of sugar by the end of the twentieth century). The link to beet is my reading of the two.

entries.label: The Everglades are drained and planted with cane
entries.hint: In 1948 the US Army Corps of Engineers begins to drain the Everglades; over the next fifty years more than half is drained, and the reclaimed Everglades Agricultural Area is given over to sugar cane by the local climate and federal subsidies. The sugar industry’s use of scarce water and its chemical run-off damage the habitat, and an effort to buy back the sugar lands for $1.7 billion has stalled.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.55; Walvin (2017) ch.11. See ec11.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: School dentists, Taiwan’s cane farmers and a wartime diary

entries.label: School dentists find the nation’s teeth corroded by sugar
entries.hint: Compulsory schooling brings every child under the scrutiny of medical and dental experts, who find alarming decay in children’s teeth; Walvin says that in the years when sugary foods and drinks came to dominate the national diet it was evident that the nation’s teeth were being corroded by sugar, a finding that generally fell on deaf political ears between the wars.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.12 (the bracket 1900–39 is mine, ‘early twentieth century’ to the eve of the war). See t1.

entries.label: Taiwan’s cane farmers under company contract
entries.hint: A Taiwanese folk song of the 1920s says ‘Sweet is Taiwan sugar, but bitter is the life of a cane farmer’: smallholders under contract could sell only to the factory in their district, at prices fixed by the mill, and local police officials harassed those who were reluctant to sign. About 80 per cent of the cane still came from individual farmers.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mazumdar (1998) pp.338 and 381 (her note 204; the song is her epigraph, the author of the song is not given).

entries.label: A Dewsbury shop assistant records the sugar ration cut
entries.hint: Kathleen Hey, a shop assistant in Dewsbury, notes in her wartime diary the groans when the rations are cut, ‘particularly sugar, which seems even more than tea to be the thing people would like more of’, and that men took the lion’s share, with two to three spoonfuls for each cup of tea — ‘men are the sugar devourers’.
entries.note: ANCHOR (as quoted): Walvin (2017) ch.12 (Hey’s diary). See c3.

events.l: The war of 1914 cuts Britain off from German beet
